heading: Bitterness and disorder: Argentina rears its ugly head in World Cup final defeat to Spain
author: Ayon Sengupta
paragraphs: Updated : Jul 27, 2026 12:40 IST , CHENNAI - 3 MINS READ
Spain’s Gavi, left, falls as he scuffles with Argentina’s Leandro Paredes (5) and Thiago Almada after the World Cup final. | Photo Credit: AP

Spain’s players formed a guard of honour as Lionel Messi walked up to collect his runners-up medal. Many embraced the 39-year-old, lingering for a moment with a player they knew had probably played a World Cup game for the last time.

As Spain’s players climbed the podium to receive their medals, the Argentine squad stood in a line with their backs turned towards the new world champions. Messi remained facing the Argentina supporters, tears streaming down his face as they serenaded him one last time. Behind him, his teammates continued to look away while Spain lifted the trophy before making a swift exit from the pitch.

The bitterness had surfaced long before the medals. Six yellow cards, Enzo Fernández’s red card and a series of confrontations after the final whistle turned defeat into disorder. Leandro Paredes grabbed Eric García by the neck before Gavi was dragged to the ground as teammates from both sides rushed in. Television pictures also appeared to show Nahuel Molina striking Rodri as Spain’s celebrations began.
Argentina players with their backs turned towards the new world champions. | Photo Credit: REUTERS

Amid the chaos, it was Lionel Scaloni who tried to restore order. The Argentina coach stepped between players, urging them apart before the confrontation could escalate further. It was an image that would repeat itself over the next hour.

When FIFA’s media obligations began, none of Argentina’s players appeared in the mixed zone or at the mandatory post-match press conference. Four years after celebrating Qatar by marching into the mixed zone singing, “Support the national team... And I don’t care what those f*****g journalists say!”, there were no songs and no players. Scaloni faced the world’s media alone.

He thanked his squad, defended them once again and accepted Spain had deserved to win. By the time he reached the mixed zone, he looked like a man carrying the grief of an entire dressing room on his shoulders. The players he had spent a month protecting were nowhere to be seen.
“Creating a group like this again is very difficult,” he said, before his voice cracked and he walked away in tears.
